chief_complaint: paroxysmal coughing fits followed by high-pitched whooping sound
hpi_details: 3-year-old boy is brought in by his parent with 2 weeks of worsening paroxysmal cough followed by an inspiratory whoop and occasional post-tussive vomiting. He attends daycare.
ideas: His parent thinks a small plastic toy piece from daycare is lodged in his windpipe and causing these violent spasms of coughing.
concerns: His parent is terrified that he will choke until he turns blue during a coughing fit or pass this violent illness to his newborn baby sister at home.
expectations: His parent hopes the doctor will take a chest X-ray to make sure his throat is clear and prescribe strong medicine to protect his infant sibling.
social_hx: Attends daycare; household includes an infant sibling.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pertussis (whooping cough) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes azithromycin, checking DTaP status, and postexposure prophylaxis for eligible close contacts.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: paroxysmal coughing fits followed by high-pitched whooping sound
Key HPI features: A 3-year-old boy presents with 2 weeks of worsening paroxysmal cough followed by an inspiratory whoop and occasional post-tussive vomiting.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Pertussis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pertussis (whooping cough).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Viral bronchitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Apnea or cyanosis during coughing fits in infants is especially dangerous.
management_principles: Azithromycin, check DTaP status, and postexposure prophylaxis for eligible close contacts
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of paroxysmal coughing fits followed by high-pitched whooping sound. HPI: pertussis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Pertussis.
reference_soap.plan: Collect a nasopharyngeal specimen for pertussis testing and start azithromycin when clinical suspicion is high. Check DTaP status, notify public health as required, and arrange postexposure prophylaxis for eligible close contacts.

must_ask.say: Can you describe the coughing spells — do they come in bursts followed by a whooping sound?
Does he vomit after the coughing fits?
Is he up to date on his DTaP vaccine?

must_ask.objective: Ask about close contacts and exposure
must_ask.say: Has anyone at home or daycare had a similar prolonged cough?

must_ask.objective: Explain the antibiotic and contact treatment plan
must_ask.say: We'll start an antibiotic course, and eligible close contacts may need preventive antibiotics to reduce spread.

history.answer: He has been having these terrible coughing fits for the past two weeks, and after coughing, he makes this loud gasping sound like he can't get any air.
It started about two weeks ago and has gotten progressively worse over the last week.
It began just like an ordinary cold with a clear runny nose and slight cough, but then the cough turned into these violent spells.
He occasionally hacks up a little bit of clear, sticky mucus, but there has been no thick yellow or green phlegm.
He has coughing fits throughout the day, but they are much worse at night and keep waking him up from sleep.
Yes, he coughs repeatedly without stopping to breathe, and at the end of the fit he makes a loud, high-pitched whooping noise as he breathes in.
Yes, after some of the hardest coughing spells, he gagged and threw up his stomach contents.
Things like crying, eating, or running around can suddenly set off another coughing fit.
He doesn't wheeze between fits, but right in the middle of a fit he struggles desperately to catch his breath.
He had a very slight fever during the first couple of days of the cold, but he has had no fever at all for over a week.
No, I haven't seen any blood in his cough, spit, or vomit.
He hasn't had night sweats, but he has been eating less because he is afraid of throwing up.
He hasn't complained of any chest pain, although he looks completely exhausted after coughing.
His nose ran for the first few days, but that stopped and he doesn't have any congestion or postnasal drip right now.
No, he has never had acid reflux or heartburn; he only vomits when he coughs so hard that he gags.
No, he doesn't get swollen legs, and he doesn't have trouble breathing lying down outside of the coughing attacks.
No, he doesn't take any blood pressure medications or heart pills.
Neither my spouse nor I smoke, and no one is permitted to smoke anywhere near him.
No one in our family or neighborhood has had tuberculosis or been treated for it.
Yes, several children in his daycare classroom have been out with prolonged, bad coughing illnesses recently.
We do not have any pets at home, and our house has no problems with mold or dust.
He has never had eczema, seasonal allergies, or asthma.
During his worst coughing spells, his face turns reddish-purple until he can gasp in air, but he hasn't passed out or stopped breathing completely.
history.topic: Episodes of turning blue or apnea

history.answer: No, there was no sudden choking incident while eating or playing; this started as a cold and slowly worsened.
We fell behind on his vaccinations when we moved last year, so he missed his toddler DTaP booster shot.
We live with my spouse and our two-month-old baby, and I'm terrified that our newborn might catch this.
He has always been healthy with no chronic medical conditions or major illnesses.
He has never been hospitalized and has never had surgery.
He takes no prescription medicines; we tried giving him children's honey cough syrup, but it didn't help at all.
He does not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
He was born full-term with no complications at delivery, and his growth and development have been right on schedule.
There is no family history of asthma, cystic fibrosis, or chronic lung conditions.

He coughs until he throws up and can't catch his breath, and I am terrified he will choke or pass whatever this is to our two-month-old baby at home. I want you to check his lungs with an X-ray to make sure nothing is stuck in there and give us a prescription to protect our newborn baby.

exam.finding: The child is alert, well-nourished, and comfortable between coughing episodes, with no retractions, nasal flaring, or stridor at rest.
Temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Clear conjunctivae without subconjunctival hemorrhages or pallor; sclerae are non-icteric.
Mild posterior pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate or cobblestoning; clear nasal mucosa without obstruction or purulent discharge.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Resonant percussion notes throughout both lung fields.
Normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops audible.
No peripheral edema of the lower extremities and no digital clubbing.
